title: Moneymore: a labelled tree under review
standfirst: The Moneymore father account is now the probable father of the established emigrant brothers Robert, Arthur and Joseph. The Corvanaghan identification and older ancestry retain their uncertainty.

status.label: Probable emigrant father; older identities open

question: Can Irish evidence identify William Walter Glasgow or reconcile the competing attached fathers?
answer: Working update, 16 October 2026: the Corvanaghan James is provisionally identified with the Moneymore James and placed under the latter’s already uncertain older James father. This inherits uncertainty in both identity and pedigree; it does not establish a mother or migration. The 1759 Drumcarn will identity and Mitchell-family alternative remain unresolved. The older William retains the selected uncertain John-3610 father. John of the Calder/Meek household is now placed under William as a possible adult identity of the 1702 child, also uncertain. This adds a Scottish family comparison, not an Irish migration record. The current Moneymore-labelled tree is not a confirmed Irish lineage. The profile formerly identified with the 1671 Kirknewton child has been separated; the older William’s parentage and claimed migration remain unproved, while later profiles rely on derivative trees and conflicting father attachments. 20 October 2026: Killycurragh gains a selected possible Kirknewton connection at 36%, and James-1025’s existing father is reassessed to 32%. The minister’s Irish father is 94% and Margaret’s is 84%; the Scottish identities remain unproved. See the linked Killycurragh generations review.

chapters.title: Nancy McClelland: an overlooked named daughter
body: Research rationale: reconcile an explicit family statement already held on Robert’s page with the lower, source-incomplete assessment on Nancy’s account.

The passage reproduced in Robert Glasgow-12’s captured and pending biography, attributed to Faris p. 18, explicitly identifies Nancy (Glasgow) McClelland and William Glasgow as children of Robert who moved to Adams County in 1805. Nancy’s distinctive married surname, established Thomas McClelland association and Virginia-to-Adams family context identify the existing daughter account. William is the independently maintained son account Glasgow-563, whose existing father assessment remains 95%. The earlier 81% review considered Nancy’s p. 34 citation and memorial without acknowledging this explicit child designation. The combined named-family and identity argument supports a 91% confident inference.

The book page itself was not inspected: the evidence actually read is a quotation attributed to Faris in a captured public WikiTree biography and preserved pending draft. The quotation, child list, memorial and later family histories may share information and are not independent corroborations. Nancy’s retained 1780/1781 birth-year discrepancy remains unresolved. No original birth, marriage, Bible, probate or migration record was newly inspected; no exact vital date or mother is newly verified. This is an existing father, already marked confident in the saved WikiTree data; there is no pending father certainty-mark change, new attachment or live save. Robert’s own proposed James father remains 35% and is not strengthened. The 91% is an individual subjective assessment, not a statistical measurement.

The proposed biography now distinguishes the current 91% research assessment from the saved WikiTree confident mark. Adding the source discussion is outstanding biography work; marking this father confident is already done.
Next: inspect Faris pp. 18 and 34 and the family authority behind them. Do not count a repeated quotation as another witness.

chapters.title: Robert and Phoebe: eight confident children, Rhoda still probable
body: Research rationale: use the already inspected family pages to test the highest-yield accessible child links, rather than repeat exhausted early source searches.

The actual Faris pp. 46–47 were visually checked. They explicitly group these children under Robert Barclay Glasgow and Phoebe McFall; Robert’s own dates, two wives and Ohio–Iowa life identify the father account. These exact percentages are subjective assessments of each complete father/profile pair, not statistical measurements.

William Harvey Glasgow: 78% → 96%. William Harvey’s full name and both dates, 27 December 1827 and 20 June 1849, match the named child in the printed family list and the existing short-lived Tranquility account. This identifies a child of this particular Robert/Phoebe family without a later adult identity gap. The memorial image and original birth/burial records remain uninspected.

Elizabeth Patton (Glasgow) Cunningham: 87% → 95%. The printed family list names Elizabeth Patton, born 1830, and her husband William Lowry Cunningham. The distinctive maiden names, year and linked William Cunningham household identify Elizabeth-2221, whose maintained account also cites Faris p. 48 and censuses. The newly inspected page explicitly supplies the paternal family role. Page46 does not supply the existing 5 February birth day/month; those fields remain unchanged and are not newly verified. The cited p. 48 and original censuses were not inspected in this batch.

Rhoda Montgomery (Glasgow) Fulton: 73% → 85%. The printed list names Rhoda Montgomery, born 31 July 1832, and husband James Fisher Fulton, matching the selected account’s names, full birth date and linked James Fulton. These combined identifiers strengthen the existing Robert father proposal. The held memorial citation instead gives Rhoda M. Fulton as 1823–1868. That nine-year disagreement is material: neither birth year nor adult/memorial identity has been resolved. Retain probable 85%, not a confident attachment, and inspect the memorial or age-bearing census next. No birth or death field changes.

Mary (Glasgow) Stewart: 88% → 94%. Faris names Mary Jane as Robert and Phoebe’s child, born 26 May 1835, with first husband Robert Stewart Glasgow and second husband John H. Stewart. The same day/month and distinctive two-husband sequence identify the existing Mary-2223 account despite its 1834 birth year. Taken together these identifiers support confident paternal inference. The 1834/1835 birth-year discrepancy remains unresolved and visible. It does not outweigh the full marital identity, but reduces confidence below a near-certain grade. Preserve 1834 in the existing vital field; no source is silently harmonized. The cited p. 89 and original censuses were not newly inspected.

Phoebe Glasgow: 79% → 96%. The family list names Phoebe Ann with the same full birth and death dates, 27 October 1837 and 13 June 1843, as the existing Tranquility child. The named parental family, full name and short lifetime identify this child particularly strongly. The Ann name is reported from the family history without changing structured name fields. The memorial image and original birth/burial entries remain uninspected.

Robert Madison Glasgow: 86% → 97%. The printed list names Robert Madison, born 16 April 1840 and died 29 January 1865 at Vicksburg, Mississippi. These exact dates, middle name and unusual death setting match Robert-2227’s military-hospital account. The same page reports Robert M. in Robert B.’s 1850 household, cohering with its explicit child list. The household and list are statements in one compilation, not independent inspected census and military proofs. The original 1850 census, Roll of Honor and memorial images remain uninspected; no military or vital field is changed.

Nancy Emeline Glasgow: 78% → 95%. Nancy Emeline’s full name and exact dates, 2 June 1843 and 5 March 1849, match the printed child list and existing short-lived Tranquility account. This specific family and lifetime identify her as the listed Robert/Phoebe child. The profile retains Ohio as birthplace, whereas the book’s narrative reports Indiana for Nancy and Susanna. That reported place discrepancy remains open; no birthplace field changes. Original birth and burial records remain uninspected.

Margaret Glasgow: 77% → 95%. Faris calls this child Sarah Margaret, born 6 November 1845, and names husband John M. Lytle. The exact date, Margaret name and linked John Lytle household identify the existing Margaret-841 account. Its female structured field and marital account also show that the biography’s male pronouns are an editorial error. Report the fuller Sarah Margaret name in the biography without changing structured name fields. Correct the male pronouns in the complete proposed draft. No birth, death or mother field changes; original records remain uninspected.

Susanna Rachel Glasgow: 87% → 96%. The printed family list names Susanna Rachel, born 5 July 1847 and died 5 May 1861 in Iowa, exactly matching this child’s maintained dates, middle name and death setting. The same account places Susanna in the reported 1850 and 1860 Robert households. This coherent identity supports the explicit paternal role. The book’s narrative reports Indiana as the birthplace of Susanna and Nancy, while this profile retains Ohio. Leave that place discrepancy open. The reported censuses are not independently inspected records, and no vital field changes.

This is one retrospective compiled family history. Its list, reported censuses, modern family fields and memorial citations may share evidence; repeated details are not independent proofs. No original birth register, census, Bible or burial record was newly inspected. The 1927 Bible provenance on p. 32 concerns William and Rhoda’s children, not the dates of Robert’s next generation; it is not transferred here. Existing named fathers remain selected. Mothers are separate, ungraded or unselected where previously so. No new parent attachment, merge or live save.

The named mother is the existing Phoebe/Phebe McFall account. Her role is recorded as source evidence, without assigning new maternal relationships or transferring father percentages to mothers. Robert’s own William father stays 94%. These are existing attachments;Unknown fathers and working topology do not change.

Seek the original family entries or independent age-bearing and named-kin records. Prioritize Rhoda’s 1823/1832 memorial conflict and retain Mary’s 1834/1835 discrepancy without silently changing either date.

chapters.title: Robert Barclay: the Bible-derived William household
body: Research rationale: test the highest-yield accessible probable father against the cited book itself and distinguish a named family from an unsourced memorial attribution.

Faris’s inspected pages 32–33 identify Robert Barclay, born 26 November 1804, among William and Rhoda’s children. The author traces their exact names and birth dates to the couple’s family Bible, held by Mrs E. R. Harvey on 25 June 1927. Page 46 matches Robert through both wives, Phoebe McFall and Matilda Jane Campbell, and his Ohio-to-Iowa life. A descendant’s dated 1928 recollection on page 47 places brothers Robert, Joseph and Madison on adjoining Ohio farms, including their father William’s former homestead. This specific provenance and complete adult identity support 94% subjective confident inference for Robert-835’s existing father, William-563.

This is a 1990 genealogy reporting earlier family evidence. The original Bible, 1928 letter and census images remain uninspected. The book, memorial and modern pedigree may share evidence. Maternal surname/date inconsistencies remain unresolved; no mother, vital field or other relationship changes. No new father attachment, merge or live save. William’s own father stays 95%; Madison’s father stays 94%. Next test: the original Bible or a contemporary probate clause.

This changes one existing father assessment from 73% probable to 94% confident inference. The other grades in Robert’s ten-person branch remain unchanged. William-563 remains a compatible alternative William in Joseph-1543’s 1831 will; this finding does not identify that beneficiary or change William-3678’s 30% father hypothesis.

chapters.title: Wythe William: a possible father, with two unresolved identities
body: Research rationale: connect the previously fatherless William/Sally branch through the specific will’s caregiving and legacy language, while testing the real competing William.

Joseph Glasgow-1543 is selected as a possible biological father of William Glasgow-3678 at 30% subjective confidence. The published 1831 will names a William Glasgow who was raised by Joseph and leaves remaining property to that William’s children. The local William/Sally household, William’s circa 1788 birth and Joseph’s birth before 1765 permit fatherhood; the unnamed 1810 Wythe male 16–25 is compatible. The newly read 1829 original confirms this married William locally but names no parent. This is an explicit working inference from a specific caregiving and testamentary family context, not a literal parent statement.

Two propositions remain unresolved: which William the will means, and whether upbringing denotes biological sonship. William Glasgow-563, born 1778, Robert-12’s son, married 1802 with children born 1803–1822, is a substantive compatible alternative will subject; Ohio residence from 1805 does not exclude earlier upbringing or a legacy. William P. Glasgow-559, born 1813, has a later known family and is a weaker comparison, not categorically excluded. The will names no wife or residence for William. It explicitly calls Arthur’s son Robert a nephew and gives him the real-estate balance and furniture; William’s children receive the remaining property, not the whole estate. A nephew or another related dependent remains a strong alternative to biological sonship. The 1810 young man is unnamed. No mother, vital date, original tree or live WikiTree attachment is changed. Joseph’s own James-1024 father remains 35%; William’s four existing child grades remain 45/54/57/89%. This 30% combines identity and biological-role uncertainty; no multiplication or measured frequency is claimed.

Original image 183 of DGS 008562846 was downloaded through the authorized viewer and read 24 October 2026. William Glasgow and Sally his wife convey 190 acres on Reed Creek, a branch of New River, Wythe County, to Stephen Sayers for $1,050. Boundaries name Isaac Brown and John Craig. Both Glasgow spouses sign/seal. James Graham and Jacob Haller certify 14 December 1829; both acknowledgments describe the deed as 8 June 1829. The opening day is faint; the earlier biography’s 3 June 1829 is retained as a date discrepancy rather than silently harmonized. Recorded 12 January 1830. The complete entry contains no named Glasgow kin, inherited-title recital or acquisition history.

Clarita H. Morgan, Births and deaths 1853–1871, on record in Pulaski County Courthouse: actual PDF p. 135, death-index p. 9 (Freeborn G section), and PDF pp. 160–161, copied death-register pp. 14–15, were visually checked. No personal William Glasgow death was located there. This is a bounded negative in a published copy, not inspection of the original county register or proof that no death entry exists. The 1859 same-surname enslaver entry on PDF p. 154, copied register p. 8, row 7, is another person’s death, not William’s death or evidence naming his parents. The reported 1865 death remains unverified; no death field is changed.
Next test: the earlier 190 acre acquisition/title or namedestate distribution must identify William’s wife, residence or children; generic surname proximity cannot resolve these alternatives.

chapters.title: Chester Samuel: a probable replacement Irish father
body: Research rationale: distinguish identifying the American estate holder from identifying his father;apply the explicit Irish sibling family to the now identified testator.

Preferred replacement father James Glasgow-1025, 67% probable, for Samuel Glasgow-2872; John Glasgow-2870 retained as an unselected 25% uncertain alternative, previously 72% probable. No mother, vital date, person merge or live attachment is changed.

Samuel-2872 is now identified with the 1824 West Fallowfield testator at 98% subjective confidence: his checked memorial names both wives Judith and Tabitha and the infant daughter Margaret Ellen, matching the original will. The newly inspected official deed index places Samuel in West Fallowfield and enters Judith Heslett in the spouse column in 1805 and 1812, with repeated Haslett dealings. These connect the already recorded Judith household to the later Tabitha estate. The will names the testator’s three brothers William, James and Robert Glasgow of Ireland; the anonymous Irish family recollection names those same three brothers with Samuel, who went to America, as children of James Glasgow and Margaret Rutherford. The distinctive sibling constellation and transatlantic division favour this particular Irish father over the current John reconstruction.

The 98% testator identification does not prove his father. 67% is a combined subjective father-profile judgement, not a multiplication of independent probabilities. Repeated family names can occur in another generation. The memorial contributes a 1761 Pennsylvania birth and a John father attribution, but no underlying birth or Bible entry has been inspected. These remain substantive competing claims. The letter account’s estimated 1726 Samuel birth, Margaret Rutherford’s estimated 1700 birth and James’s supposed 1759 death are consequential conflicts if established; no date is adjusted to force the preferred route. The 1759 Drumcarn testator’s identification with James-1025 remains unproved. Samuel-1492 remains the separate letter-defined account, father 76%, with possible duplicate identity, not a proved second son or a merge. Mary Cranmer’s existing maternal attachment is not reassessed or transferred to Margaret Rutherford. The current Find a Grave family links and the compiled Bible narrative are claims, not inspected original parent entries. The deed originals remain unread; Judith Heslett is the index’s spouse-column wording, not an established maiden surname.

Visually inspected official index, PDF p.940, on 24 October 2026. Hugh Glasgow of Fawn, York County is indexed as 1799 grantor to Timothy Currens for East & West Nottingham property,H-3:253. Samuel’s West Fallowfield entries are 1804 purchase from John Sweeny,A-3:435; 1805 purchase from William Haslett,A-3:433; 1805 sale to Abraham Rackstraw,Y-2:391; and 1812 sale to James Haslett,K-3:394. Judith Heslett appears in the spouse column for the two sales, with et.al.; her maiden name and the original parties’ precise capacities are not established. The separate1804 East Fallowfield Samuel/Daniel Kent,Y-2:16, remains an unassigned namesake comparison. These are separate indexed transactions, not independent confirmations of parentage. Original deed clauses and image-page offsets remain unverified. H-3 was verified as Deed Book Vol.056,portal Doc771593; full images/print invoked HTTP authentication and were not read.

Next test:read the actual York family-Bible birth/parent entry and secure the burial-age reading;then the Haslett-related title recitals. A genuine1761 birth/parent statement could overturn the preferred Irish-generation reconstruction.

chapters.title: The Irish letter’s four sons: four probable father links
body: Research rationale: apply the complete named family account consistently across the four brothers, distinguishing it from the unproved American-emigrant connection.

Father James-1025, specifically the James/Margaret Rutherford family-account role: James-1024 18%→78%, Samuel-1492 23%→76%, Robert-2425 18%→77%, William-2426 46%→84%, all now probable. The American Robert-12/Arthur-649/Joseph-1543 father grades remain35%, John-4027 remains30%, Mary-4030 remains22%; James-1025’s own William-1026 father remains32%.

The anonymous family recollection printed by Faris on p.9 explicitly gives James Glasgow, husband of Margaret Rutherford, four sons: William, Robert, James who settled near Moneymore, and Samuel who went to America, plus daughter Ellen. The letter-defined father is the family role represented by James-1025. These are specific named relationships, substantially stronger than the contributed-tree and locality summaries used by the earlier percentages. The same full-letter tradition was already read on 20 October; actual Faris pages now confirm its full structure. Its reproduction by Albert Rutherford and Faris’s pedigree are dependent presentations, not independent witnesses.

James-1024 is reviewed as the letter-defined son who settled near Moneymore. The father James and son James occupy explicitly distinct generations in that account; the earlier possibility that these two family roles were one duplicated adult no longer deserves the same weight. The 78% assessment does not identify the son with the Corvanaghan householder or make him father of the American emigrant Robert.

Samuel-1492 is reviewed as the letter-defined emigrant son. The independently inspected 1824 West Fallowfield will names brothers William, James and Robert of Ireland, a distinctive match to that sibling set. This supports the family reconstruction while the testator’s profile identity remains open. Samuel-2872 is another compatible account, retained without merge or exclusion; its Pennsylvania birth and John/Mary Cranmer parentage need independent examination. The 76% is the complete father proposition for the letter-defined Samuel, not proof of his Gorteen identity or a new assessment of Samuel-2872.

Robert-2425 is the inherited James/Margaret Rutherford son account, matching the letter’s named Robert, himself described as a William Glasgow’s father. This specific position in the named sibling family supports 77%, while his adult life remains little anchored. His imported United States death location is not established by the letter or by the will’s Ireland designation.

William-2426 already represents the letter’s maternal-grandfather family role and is assessed as Margaret, wife of the Coleraine minister’s father at 84%. The same letter explicitly names his own father James and mother Margaret Rutherford. Reconcile this previously underused explicit relationship at 84%; do not transfer it to the distinct Cunningham husband or treat the imported circa1829 United States death as established.

These are probable, not confident, relationships reconstructed from an anonymous retrospective family recollection, with no newly inspected parent register. The original letter remains uninspected. Faris calls the anonymous recollection file5 within PRONI T1959, while Rutherford’s reproduced copy cites T1959/3; retain this reference discrepancy pending archive checking. The 1759 probate index says Drumcarn and names no kin; neither that testator nor the inherited life dates are identified by this reassessment. The letter calls William eldest although the imported sibling birth estimates put him later; those estimates remain unverified. Faris also flags Samuel’s infant daughter and surviving mother-in-law in1824 against the supposed early paternal death. Those tensions require testing, not automatic exclusion. Preserve all existing people, vital fields, maternal grades and alternatives. No Scottish migration, identity merge, live edit or new father attachment is claimed.

Faris, The Glasgow Family of Adams County, Ohio (1990), printed pp.8–12, DGS007834162, images1564–1566, inspected23October2026; reassessed24October. Original Chester County estate7520, will17May1824, proved31May1824, portal Doc773006 pp588–589, previously visually read in the project on23October; that reading is reused, not a new inspection.

chapters.title: James of Moneymore: actual book leaves the father uncertain
body: Research rationale: inspect the actual genealogy and distinguish its parentage argument from the stronger sibling evidence.

Existing father-profile propositions only: Robert-12 85% → 35%; Arthur-649 and Joseph-1543 each 82% → 35%; John-4027 76% → 30%; Mary-4030 64% → 22%. All five were probable; the first four are now possible and Mary uncertain. James-1024 remains the selected named candidate; no attachment is removed. The separate Irish-family review on24October subsequently assesses James-1024’s father78% and Samuel-1492’s father76%; the American father grades here are unchanged.

The actual Faris book has now been inspected, rather than only its catalogue abstract. Printed p.11 uses a dotted possible connection from James of Moneymore to the American brothers; p.12 explicitly reports that evidence for Robert and his brothers’ parentage had not been found. James was the author’s identifiable County Londonderry candidate, not an evidenced father. The retrospective Irish pedigree on pp.8–9 and Samuel’s 1824 Pennsylvania will discussed on p.12 identify an Irish sibling group, including William, James and Robert remaining in Ireland, without joining it to the emigrant brothers. County setting, a compatible generation and the existing family tradition keep James a plausible candidate, but cannot sustain the earlier probable father assessment.

Mary’s case additionally depends on identifying the 1779 will witness Mary Arter as the emigrant sister. Faris p.13 transmits an unnamed sister styled Mrs Arthur; p.15 identifies Mary Arter with that sister through the tax/probate cluster, rather than an explicit sibling or birth statement. The association remains positive but does not establish her father.

Robert, Arthur and Joseph’s established brotherhood remains separately supported by the maintained 1806 letter transcription and Joseph’s 1831 will. John of Peters Township remains a probable brother at 83%; Faris p.15 also reconstructs the four brothers from the 1779–1780 tax/probate cluster. These sibling arguments do not identify their father. The 1824 Samuel will has been read only through Faris’s excerpt, not its manuscript. The Irish Robert in that will/pedigree is not identified as the emigrant Robert born in 1749. All mothers, upstream ancestry, life dates and current attachments are preserved; no live WikiTree save or identity merge follows. Exact percentages are subjective pair-specific judgments, not measured frequencies or multiplied probabilities.

Faris p.12 abstracts Samuel Glasgow of West Fallowfield, Chester County, Pennsylvania: will dated 17 May 1824 and proved 31 May 1824, daughter Margaret Ellen Glasgow, with the residue to sons of his brothers William, James and Robert in Ireland. This is a useful compatible identity lead for the already existing Samuel-1492 account, whose contributed Irish family has the same brother pattern, not a proved identification. The manuscript, daughter’s records and migration/estate continuity remain to be checked. No independent birth age is supplied. Keep the Irish brother Robert distinct from Robert-12; do not infer the American emigrants’ father from this will. Samuel-1492’s father probability remains 23%.

David Faris, The Glasgow Family of Adams County, Ohio (Baltimore: Gateway Press, 1990), printed pp.8–15; FamilySearch catalogue koha:646654, film 2055438 Item 5, DGS 007834162, images 1564–1567, visually inspected 23 October 2026. This is an inspected published genealogy, not inspection of its cited original letters or wills. The film’s generic Tennessee metadata does not describe this book item. The letters are cross-referenced on p.13 to pp.20–21; those pages were not inspected in this batch, so the maintained letter transcription remains the source for its wording.

Glasgow-4028 and Glasgow-4029 are the existing record-defined daughter and son accounts, not speculative later adult identifications. Assess John as their father at 98% each, strongly supported by the explicit abstracted relationship and matching will context. The manuscript has not been inspected, so this does not certify the spelling or completeness of the abstract. Joseph the son is distinct from the adult Joseph who witnessed the will.

The original will and probate packet remain uninspected. The checked abstract gives 1779, not the execution/probate days; existing 14 March and 3 September date limits are preserved from the earlier cited profile account, not newly verified. The will index verifies John’s locator, Cumberland Will Book C, p.161, but supplies no relatives. Ann is named as wife, not expressly mother of the children; her existing maternal attachments remain unassessed. Nancy (Glascoe) Wright is only a possible identification of Agnes: an approximately 1778 birth fits a child alive in 1779 and Agnes/Nancy can be compatible name forms, but the later Maryland/Indiana household has no inspected parent, guardianship or estate bridge to Peters Township. Her existing John father is therefore possible at 37%, not confident. The witness Joseph is not proved to be Joseph of Wythe County. The family-history article may depend on Faris and is not independent corroboration of his genealogy. The older James-1025 father of James-1024 remains 18%; no Scottish migration, Mary Harkness maternity, new mother, identity merge or live edit follows. Exact percentages express individual subjective judgments, not measured frequencies or multiplied independent probabilities.

Faris p.15 has now been inspected and explicitly reconstructs this Peters Township group, including Mary Arter. It is a secondary reconstruction, not a newly inspected will manuscript. His family-tradition source on p.13 leaves the sister’s forename unstated. The earlier 98% child-role and 83% brother assessments are unchanged.

chapters.title: Corvanaghan and Moneymore: a conditional James family
body: Glasgow-1025 is selected as the very uncertain working father of Glasgow-2988, the 1766 Corvanaghan householder, through preferred provisional identity with Glasgow-1024 of Moneymore. The existing Corvanaghan biography already retains the Moneymore man as a compatible candidate: the places are roughly nine miles apart, the name matches and their circa 1720/1722 births are estimates rather than a real two-year conflict. The 1766 Irish occurrence can precede the compiled 1770 immigration claim associated with the Moneymore family; no post 1766 Irish occurrence has been assigned to the Corvanaghan man. This is a weak locality and chronology preference, not proof of emigration or identity. The older James is already an uncertain father in the Moneymore pedigree. Extending that attachment gives the Corvanaghan account a conditional place in the same family, without inventing an intermediate generation. It inherits two major uncertainties: adult identity and the older pedigree itself.

The older James account’s circa 1700 birth would allow an ordinary father–son interval of about 20–22 years, if the estimates are close. Those guessed years do not independently establish paternity. No contemporary record names the older James as father of either Moneymore James or the Corvanaghan householder. The current older-father attachment is a tree hypothesis, not a clause in the 1766 return, the pension record or the later family history. The older and younger James accounts might themselves be duplicates rather than father and son; if that identity is established, this additional father edge must collapse with it. Their existing Scottish ancestral attachments receive no new support. No mother is selected: the uncertain Rutherford attachment on the Moneymore account is not independently supported for the Corvanaghan man and is not copied.

The 1766 Kildress return names James Glasgow as a Protestant householder at Corvanaghan. It gives no age, birthplace, wife, children, occupation or father. The two sons currently attached as Glasgow-2989 and Glasgow-2990 remain unproved, with their existing grades and dates unchanged. Their estimated generations cannot identify the householder. Corvanaghan is distinct from Gortnavreeghan in County Cavan; the rejected Cavan lease assignment is not restored. The 1740 Derryloran return contains two James and two William householders without townlands or kinship, and the 1766 Derryloran return separately names two Jas. Glasgo at Drumearn. None is newly assigned to a particular generation.

Faris’s later genealogy calls Glasgow-12’s father James of Moneymore, but the underlying evidence for that father identification has not been inspected. Robert’s 1834 pension declaration gives County Derry birth in 1749 and arrival in Virginia in 1769; it does not name parents or siblings. The fuller Mary Harkness and sibling package, the compiled 1770 entry and the 1804 same-name naturalisation applicant remain separate inherited claims. The reported departure of a mother and elder brothers by 1766 does not independently place their father in America that year. No new wife, emigrant child, ship, naturalisation identity or extreme-age death is attached to the Corvanaghan account. The 1766 return and the later Moneymore family tradition may still concern different men.

Glasgow-1970 of the Mitchell-family tradition remains a live alternative identity for the Corvanaghan householder. The 1879 Hillsdale history describes a Scotsman and his Mitchell wife moving to the Cookstown area about 1750, with a son John and later Michigan descendants. It does not name Corvanaghan. The Moneymore route is preferred only weakly for its more specific nearby locality and compatible 1766 window; the Mitchell account is not excluded, and the birthplaces on the compared profiles are not independent proof. Another local James remains possible. The absence of Glasgow occupiers at Corvanaghan in the 1826 tithe list, sixty years later, does not establish death or emigration.

The 1759 will reference does not prove this father generation. The previously reviewed PRONI detail names Drumcarn, not Drumearn, and supplies no age or kin. It may concern the older account, the Moneymore James or another namesake. The meaning of 17 January 1759 and the testator’s modern profile identity remain unresolved. No 1759 death, estate event or residence is transferred to the 1766 Corvanaghan householder. The older profile’s structured dates and places are retained as existing fields with those qualifications; the new parent model does not resolve them.

One very uncertain father is newly selected through a possible Moneymore identity and an already uncertain older pedigree. No mother, source-proved parentage, migration, merge, vital-field change, original inspection, live WikiTree edit or confidence upgrade is claimed. The compared James accounts remain separate and may be duplicates rather than distinct brothers or generations. Working connectivity counts retained accounts and does not independently validate those identities. Full comparisons containing living-person references remain private; the historical findings and relationships remain public.

chapters.period: 1702–1755 · possible Scottish son of the older William
chapters.title: A selected uncertain Calder son, with Irish identity still open
body: Select William Glasgow-1026 as the uncertain working father of John Glasgow-3481, the combined Calder father account recorded in 1730 and with Christian Meek in 1751–1755. This adopts possible identity with John Glasgow-1544, the child indexed at Kirknewton in 1702 with father William. The same name and parish and a normal adult generation favour this concrete child account over an unidentified origin: if baptised near birth in 1702, he would be about 28 in 1730 and 53 at the 1755 child. Those ages are conditional examples, not ages stated in the registers. The old circa 1710 birth was inferred from assumed age at the 1730 fatherhood and cannot exclude the 1702 child. The child’s existing father identity as William-1026 is itself qualified; no record explicitly identifies the later Meek husband as his son.

John-1544 and John-3481 remain separate profile accounts of a possible single man; the selection does not establish two distinct John sons. The 1702 date remains unreconciled: the child’s field uses a before 11 November boundary while its biography cites a 29 November baptism. Neither date is newly corrected. The later account combines the 1730 father of Jean, whose mother is omitted, with the 1751 and 1755 Meek household. That earlier adult identification remains a preferred working combination, not a continuous household proved by occupation, land or witnesses. John-81, estimated born 1709, remains a specific competing identity for the 1730 father. His Guthrie household is indexed with children in West Calder in 1751 and 1753 while the Meek household appears in Kirknewton in 1751 and Leith in 1755. That concrete overlap makes a simple succession of wives less persuasive; do not combine the full Guthrie and Meek families without resolving the entries. No birth estimate alone excludes John-81. Other local John origins remain possible. Ann McCook is not selected as John-3481’s mother: the reviewed 1702 child citation names William, and the attached Ann field does not supply an independently verified maternal clause. William’s existing uncertain John-3610 father and older family alternatives retain their grades; no date or family field is changed to force the new route.

This new son proposal does not establish the older William’s Irish migration or his identity in an Irish record. The current Moneymore lineage and all competing father assignments retain their existing uncertainty.

body: The 1671 Kirknewton baptism names William, son of Andrew Glasgow. It cannot be the father of a child baptised in 1682, because he would have been ten.
The older William now represents a reconstructed Kirknewton household; that household identity and its parents still need original-record testing.

chapters.title: No demonstrated Irish bridge
body: No inspected record places the older William, spouse or children at Moneymore. The 1740 Derryloran return records local Glasgow households, but it does not identify this family.
A 1759 probate index for a James at Drumearn is useful local evidence, not a parentage or migration record.

Working connection added on 20 October 2026: the letter’s older Killycurragh William is tentatively identified with the 1705 Kirknewton child William Glasgow-1318. This places the Cunningham husband under him at 36%, while James Glasgow-1025’s existing father Glasgow-1026 rises from 12% to 32%. The letter explicitly supplies brothers James, John and William under an older William; the compatible Scottish baptisms support a non-exclusive cluster comparison. The Irish documentary father of Rev. John of Coleraine is assessed at 94%, and Margaret’s father William Glasgow-2426 at 84%. The two Irish grandfathers William remain separate. No Scottish migration, adult identity or 1759 testator identity is proved; the circa-1735 estimate for William-2426 also conflicts with the letter’s eldest-son description and remains unchanged pending evidence.

chapters.title: The Hawthorne nephew is a real record, but which James?
body: Research rationale: test the previously unverified nephew theory associated with James-3305, without using a same-name record to manufacture an emigrant brother or a parent.

The inspected Betham manuscript abstract names James Hawthorne of Downpatrick, County Down, and dates his will 20 November 1760, followed by the probate annotation 29 January 1762. The entry begins on handwritten page 136 and continues on page 137, where it expressly says “Nephew — James Glasgow”. The Glasgow surname and nephew relationship are legible. The abstract supplies no age, residence, occupation, wife, children or parents for the nephew. Downpatrick is the testator’s locality, not an established residence for James Glasgow. This is an original image of Betham’s later abstract, not the original will.

Glasgow-3305 is the existing compatible candidate because its maintained research already identifies this very Hawthorne-nephew theory. The abstract now verifies the documentary nephew, but provides no identifier joining him to the Moneymore-labelled profile, the 1766 Drumearn householders, the 1775 Cookstown petitioner or the emigrant brothers. Other contemporary Irish James Glasgows are not excluded by missing fields. Retain this record on the existing candidate account; do not create a duplicate or select a new parent. James-1024 remains the uncertain father at 12%; Mary Harkness remains independently unproved. The kin term alone does not identify which parent or marriage produced the relationship, so it cannot supply a named Hawthorne mother.

Identify the nephew through a fuller surviving Hawthorne will, estate distribution, or a deed/church record naming his parent, residence or another distinctive relative. Compare that identifier with the Cookstown/Drumearn and emigrant-family evidence before changing a father assessment. Full-will survival remains unresolved; the Betham-abstract access question is closed. No father-confidence or connectivity increase is counted.
